tool.name: Linux
tool.tagline: Using and administering Linux systems from the command line
tool.description: Linux is the operating system behind most servers, cloud instances, containers and embedded devices. This curriculum covers working with it from the command line: the filesystem, users and permissions, processes and services, packages, logs, networking and storage, up to the kernel features (namespaces and cgroups) that containers are built on. It is the practical foundation for DevOps, backend and infrastructure work.

concepts.name: Kernel, distributions and the shell
concepts.summary: What Linux actually is: the kernel, the userland on top of it, and how distributions package them.
concepts.why: Knowing which layer you are dealing with tells you where to look for docs, logs and fixes.
concepts.body:
Strictly speaking, **Linux is a kernel**: the core program that manages CPU scheduling, memory, devices, filesystems and networking, and that every other program asks for services through **system calls**. What people call "a Linux system" is the kernel plus a **userland**: the GNU core utilities (`ls`, `cp`, `grep`), a C library, a shell such as bash, an init system (almost always **systemd** today) and thousands of other programs.

A **distribution** bundles all of that with a package manager, default configuration and a release policy. The big families:

- **Debian / Ubuntu**: `apt` and `.deb` packages, popular on servers and in cloud images,
- **Fedora / RHEL / Rocky / Alma**: `dnf` and `.rpm` packages, common in enterprises,
- **Arch**, **Alpine** (tiny, musl libc, popular for containers), **SUSE** and others.

The commands in this curriculum work across distributions; package names, some paths and the default firewall differ. `/etc/os-release` tells you which distribution you are on and `uname -r` which kernel.

You interact with a Linux server mainly through a **shell** over SSH: there is usually no desktop. Everything is text, configuration lives in files under `/etc`, and almost every task can be scripted, which is exactly why Linux dominates servers and the cloud.
concepts.code:
uname -sr                     # Linux 6.12.0-...   (kernel name and release)
head -n 2 /etc/os-release     # PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS" / NAME="Ubuntu"
hostnamectl                   # host name, OS, kernel, architecture (systemd)
uptime                        # up 3 days, 2 users, load average: 0.15, 0.10, 0.05
whoami                        # ada
echo "$SHELL"                 # /bin/bash
nproc                         # 4   (CPU cores)
free -h | head -n 2           # memory total / used / available
takeaways: Linux is the kernel; a distribution adds userland, packages and defaults
Debian/Ubuntu use apt, Fedora/RHEL use dnf
/etc/os-release and uname -r identify the system
pitfalls: Searching for help without saying which distribution you run; package names and paths differ.

quiz.q: What does the Linux kernel itself provide?
options: Process scheduling, memory, devices and system calls
quiz.explain: The kernel manages hardware and resources; shells, package managers and desktops are userland.

quiz.q: Which file tells you the distribution and its version?
quiz.explain: /etc/os-release is the standard, machine-readable description of the distribution.

concepts.name: The filesystem hierarchy
concepts.summary: One tree rooted at /: what lives in /etc, /var, /home, /usr, /tmp, /proc and /dev.
concepts.why: Knowing the standard layout means you can find any config file or log on a machine you have never seen.
concepts.body:
Linux has a single directory tree starting at `/` (the **root**). There are no drive letters: other disks are **mounted** at directories inside the tree. The layout follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard:

- `/etc`: system-wide **configuration** (text files),
- `/var`: variable data such as **logs** (`/var/log`), caches, spools and databases (`/var/lib`),
- `/home/<user>`: users' files; `/root` is root's home,
- `/usr`: installed programs and libraries (`/usr/bin`, `/usr/lib`); `/usr/local` for software you install by hand; on modern distributions `/bin` and `/lib` are just symlinks into `/usr`,
- `/opt`: self-contained third-party applications,
- `/tmp`: temporary files, often cleaned at boot and sometimes stored in RAM,
- `/boot`: the kernel and bootloader files,
- `/dev`: **device files** such as disks (`/dev/sda`, `/dev/nvme0n1`) and `/dev/null`,
- `/proc` and `/sys`: **virtual** filesystems where the kernel exposes processes and hardware as files,
- `/run`: runtime state such as PID files and sockets, cleared at boot,
- `/mnt` and `/media`: mount points for extra or removable disks.

The Unix idea that "everything is a file" shows up everywhere: devices, process information and kernel settings are all read and written with ordinary file tools.
concepts.code:
ls /
# bin boot dev etc home lib media mnt opt proc root run srv sys tmp usr var
ls -ld /bin                 # lrwxrwxrwx ... /bin -> usr/bin   (merged /usr)
ls /etc | head -n 3         # system-wide configuration files
ls /var/log | head -n 3     # log files
cat /proc/loadavg           # kernel data presented as a file
ls -l /dev/null             # crw-rw-rw- ... /dev/null   (c = character device)
echo ~ "$HOME"              # /home/ada /home/ada
takeaways: One tree from /; other disks are mounted into it
Config in /etc, logs and data in /var, programs in /usr
/proc, /sys and /dev expose the kernel and devices as files
pitfalls: Storing application data in /tmp, which may be wiped at reboot.

quiz.q: Where would you look first for a service's log files written to disk?
quiz.explain: Variable data such as logs lives under /var, conventionally /var/log.

quiz.q: What is special about /proc?
options: It is a virtual filesystem generated by the kernel
quiz.explain: Files in /proc are generated on the fly by the kernel to expose process and system information.

concepts.name: Navigating and managing files
concepts.summary: Move around with cd and ls, and create, copy, move, find and delete files and directories.
concepts.why: These dozen commands are what you type most on any Linux machine.
concepts.body:
Paths are **absolute** when they start with `/` and **relative** to the current directory otherwise. `.` is the current directory, `..` its parent and `~` your home. `pwd` prints where you are, `cd dir` moves, `cd` alone goes home and `cd -` returns to the previous directory.

`ls` lists a directory: `-l` long format (permissions, owner, size, date), `-a` includes hidden **dotfiles**, `-h` human-readable sizes, `-t` sorts by time. File names are case-sensitive, and extensions mean nothing to the system.

Managing files:

- `mkdir -p a/b/c` creates nested directories, `touch f` creates an empty file,
- `cp src dst` copies (`-r` for directories, `-a` to preserve permissions and times),
- `mv src dst` moves **or renames**,
- `rm f` deletes, `rm -r dir` deletes recursively, `rmdir` removes empty directories.

There is **no trash can**: `rm` is permanent. Use `-i` to be asked, double-check globs with `ls` first, and never run `rm -rf` with a variable that might be empty.

`find` searches a tree by name, type, size or age: `find . -name '*.log' -mtime +7` lists logs older than a week; add `-delete` or `-exec` to act on them. `tree` (if installed) draws a directory tree.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
pwd                              # /tmp/tmp.Xyz
mkdir -p project/src/utils       # -p: create parents, no error if present
touch project/README.md
cp project/README.md project/README.bak
mv project/README.bak project/notes.md   # move = rename
ls -la project                   # long listing, hidden files included
cp -r project project-copy       # -r for directories
rm -r project-copy               # recursive delete: there is no undo
find . -name '*.md' | sort       # ./project/README.md ./project/notes.md
find . -type d -empty            # ./project/src/utils
cd project/src && cd ../..       # .. is the parent directory
cd - >/dev/null && pwd           # back to the previous directory
takeaways: Absolute paths start with /; . is here, .. is the parent, ~ is home
cp -r and rm -r for directories; mv also renames
rm is permanent; find searches by name, type, size and age
pitfalls: Running `rm -rf "$DIR"/*` when DIR is empty, which expands to /*.

quiz.q: What does `mv report.txt final.txt` do in the same directory?
options: Fails because final.txt does not exist
Moves it to a directory named final.txt only
quiz.explain: mv to a new name in the same directory is a rename.

quiz.q: Which command lists files under the current directory with names ending in .log?
quiz.explain: find walks the tree recursively and -name matches a glob against each file name.

concepts.name: Viewing files and searching text
concepts.summary: Read files with cat, less, head and tail, follow logs live and search them with grep.
concepts.why: Reading configs and logs is most of what troubleshooting a server looks like.
concepts.body:
Choose the viewer by file size and purpose:

- `cat file` prints a small file in one go,
- `less file` pages through anything, however large: Space and b to move, `/text` to search, `n` for the next match, `G` for the end, `q` to quit,
- `head -n 20` and `tail -n 20` show the beginning or end,
- `tail -f app.log` **follows** a file, printing new lines as they are written; `tail -F` keeps following across log rotation.

`grep pattern files` prints matching lines. Common flags: `-i` ignore case, `-n` line numbers, `-r` recursive through directories, `-v` invert (lines that do **not** match), `-c` count, `-l` only file names, `-E` extended regexes, `-C 3` three lines of context. Combine them with pipes: `grep -v '^#' sshd_config | grep -v '^$'` shows a config without comments and blank lines.

`wc -l` counts lines, `file` identifies what a file actually contains (text, ELF binary, gzip...), and `diff a b` compares two files. Compressed logs can be read without unpacking using `zcat`, `zless` and `zgrep`.

Do not `cat` binary files or huge logs into the terminal; use `less` or `head`. Files you cannot read give "Permission denied", which often means you need `sudo`.
concepts.code:
cat /etc/hostname                 # print a small file
less /var/log/syslog              # page: / search, n next, G end, q quit
head -n 3 /etc/passwd             # first 3 lines
tail -n 20 /var/log/nginx/error.log
tail -F /var/log/nginx/access.log # follow new lines, survive rotation
wc -l /etc/passwd                 # 32 /etc/passwd
grep -n '^root' /etc/passwd       # 1:root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
grep -ri 'timeout' /etc/nginx/    # recursive, case-insensitive
grep -v '^#' /etc/ssh/sshd_config | grep -v '^$'   # config without comments
grep -c ' 500 ' access.log        # count server errors
zgrep 'error' /var/log/syslog.2.gz
file /usr/bin/ls                  # ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64 ...
takeaways: less for big files, head/tail for ends, tail -f to follow
grep -i -n -r -v -c cover most searches
zcat, zless and zgrep read compressed logs
pitfalls: Opening a multi-gigabyte log with cat or a text editor instead of less or tail.

quiz.q: Which command shows new log lines as they are written?
quiz.explain: tail -f keeps the file open and prints appended lines.

quiz.q: What does `grep -v '^#' file` output?
quiz.explain: -v inverts the match, so comment lines are filtered out.

concepts.name: Users, groups and root
concepts.summary: How Linux identifies users and groups, what root is, and how sudo grants admin rights safely.
concepts.why: Every permission decision, service account and sudo prompt is based on users and groups.
concepts.body:
Every process runs as a **user** with a numeric **UID** and belongs to a primary **group** (GID) plus any number of supplementary groups. Names are just labels for these numbers. `id` shows yours; `whoami` just the name.

Accounts are defined in plain text files:

- `/etc/passwd`: one line per user, `name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell`,
- `/etc/shadow`: password hashes, readable only by root,
- `/etc/group`: groups and their members.

`getent passwd name` and `getent group name` query them, including accounts from LDAP or other directories.

**root** (UID 0) bypasses permission checks and can do anything, which is exactly why you should not work as root. Instead, administrators use **sudo** to run a single command with root privileges: `sudo apt update`. sudo asks for **your own** password, checks the rules in `/etc/sudoers` (often "members of the `sudo` or `wheel` group may run anything"), and logs every command. `sudo -i` opens a root shell when you really need several commands; `su - user` switches user with that user's password.

Besides people, systems have many **system users** (UIDs below 1000) such as `www-data`, `postgres` or `nobody`. Services run as these unprivileged users so a compromised service cannot take over the whole machine.
concepts.code:
whoami                     # ada
id                         # uid=1000(ada) gid=1000(ada) groups=1000(ada),27(sudo),998(docker)
grep '^ada:' /etc/passwd   # ada:x:1000:1000:Ada,,,:/home/ada:/bin/bash
getent group sudo          # sudo:x:27:ada
sudo -l                    # which commands may I run with sudo?
sudo apt update            # one command as root (asks for YOUR password)
sudo -i                    # root login shell; type exit to leave
su - bob                   # become bob (needs bob's password)
ps -o user= -p "$(pgrep -o nginx)"   # nginx master runs as root, workers as www-data
takeaways: Users and groups are numbers (UID/GID); root is UID 0
/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group define accounts
Use sudo for single admin commands rather than working as root
pitfalls: Running everything as root, so one typo or compromised script can destroy the system.

quiz.q: Whose password does `sudo` ask for by default?
quiz.explain: sudo authenticates you and then checks /etc/sudoers to see what you may run.

quiz.q: Why do services like nginx workers run as www-data instead of root?
options: To limit the damage if the service is compromised
quiz.explain: An unprivileged account confines what an attacker who takes over the process can do.

concepts.name: File permissions: chmod and chown
concepts.summary: Read rwx permission strings, change them with symbolic and octal chmod, and change ownership with chown.
concepts.why: Permission errors are the most common Linux problem, and wrong permissions are a common security hole.
concepts.body:
Every file has an **owner**, a **group** and three permission sets: for the **user** (owner), the **group** and **others**. `ls -l` shows them as a string like `-rwxr-x---`: the first character is the type (`-` file, `d` directory, `l` symlink), then three `rwx` triplets.

For **files**, `r` allows reading, `w` writing and `x` executing. For **directories** the meaning differs: `r` lists the names, `w` creates, deletes and renames entries, and `x` allows entering and accessing items inside. A directory usually needs `r` and `x` together.

`chmod` changes permissions in two notations:

- **symbolic**: `chmod u+x script.sh`, `chmod go-w file`, `chmod u=rw,g=r,o= file`,
- **octal**: each triplet is a digit with r=4, w=2, x=1, so `chmod 644` is rw-r--r--, `755` rwxr-xr-x, `600` rw-------, `750` rwxr-x---.

`chown user:group file` changes ownership (root only); `chown -R` recurses, and `chgrp` changes just the group. Use `-R` with care: making a whole tree executable or world-writable is a classic mistake.

Typical settings: scripts `755`, private keys `600` (SSH refuses keys that are too open), config with secrets `640` owned by root and the service's group, web content readable but not writable by the web server user.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
touch script.sh notes.txt
ls -l script.sh                  # -rw-r--r-- 1 ada ada 0 ... script.sh
chmod +x script.sh               # add execute (filtered by your umask)
chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o= script.sh
stat -c '%A %a %n' script.sh     # -rwxr-x--- 750 script.sh
chmod 640 notes.txt
stat -c '%A %a %n' notes.txt     # -rw-r----- 640 notes.txt
mkdir shared && chmod 750 shared # dirs: x = may enter, r = may list
stat -c '%A %a %n' shared        # drwxr-x--- 750 shared
# sudo chown ada:developers notes.txt     # owner and group
# sudo chown -R www-data: /var/www/site   # recursive; "user:" = user's login group
takeaways: rwx for user, group, others; octal r=4 w=2 x=1
On directories x means enter, r means list, w means create/delete
chown user:group changes ownership; be careful with -R
pitfalls: Fixing a permission error with chmod 777, which lets every user modify the file.

quiz.q: What does chmod 640 give a file?
A user can list a directory's names but gets 'Permission denied' opening any file inside. Which bit is missing on the directory?
quiz.explain: x on a directory is needed to access the entries inside it; r only lists names.

concepts.name: Processes: ps, top and friends
concepts.summary: Every running program is a process with a PID and a parent; list and monitor them with ps, top and pgrep.
concepts.why: Finding what is running, what eats CPU or memory and what started what is everyday Linux work.
concepts.body:
A **process** is a running instance of a program. Each has a **PID**, a parent (**PPID**), an owner, a state and its own memory. Processes form a tree: PID 1 (**systemd** on most systems) is the ancestor of everything, and every process is started by another one forking. `$$` in bash is the shell's own PID.

Listing processes:

- `ps` alone shows processes in your terminal; `ps aux` (BSD style) or `ps -ef` (System V style) show all of them,
- `ps -o pid,ppid,user,%cpu,%mem,stat,etime,cmd` picks the columns,
- `ps -ef --forest` or `pstree` show the parent/child tree,
- `pgrep -a name` finds PIDs by name, `pidof prog` by exact program name.

`top` (or the friendlier `htop`) shows a live view sorted by CPU; in top, press `M` to sort by memory, `P` for CPU, `k` to kill and `q` to quit. The header shows uptime, **load average**, task counts and memory.

Process states in the `STAT` column: `R` running or runnable, `S` sleeping (waiting for something, the normal state), `D` uninterruptible sleep (usually waiting on disk or network storage), `T` stopped, `Z` **zombie** (finished, but its parent has not collected the exit status yet). A few zombies are harmless; a growing number points to a buggy parent.
concepts.code:
echo $$                               # PID of this shell
ps                                    # processes of this terminal
ps aux | head -n 3                    # USER PID %CPU %MEM VSZ RSS TTY STAT START TIME COMMAND
ps -ef --forest | tail -n 5           # parent/child tree
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,etime,cmd -p $$   # chosen columns for one PID
pgrep -a sshd                         # PIDs and command lines by name
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 5       # top memory users
top                                   # live view: M memory, P CPU, q quit
takeaways: Each process has a PID, a parent and an owner; PID 1 is systemd
ps aux / ps -ef list everything; pgrep finds by name
STAT: R running, S sleeping, D waiting on I/O, Z zombie
pitfalls: Reading `ps aux | grep nginx` and counting the grep process itself as a match; use pgrep.

quiz.q: What does a process in state D usually indicate?
options: It is waiting uninterruptibly, typically on disk or network I/O
quiz.explain: D is uninterruptible sleep; it cannot even be killed until the I/O completes.

quiz.q: Which process is the ancestor of all others on a typical modern distribution?
quiz.explain: The kernel starts PID 1, usually systemd, which starts everything else.

concepts.name: Signals and stopping processes
concepts.summary: Ask processes to stop or reload with signals: SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGINT, SIGHUP, SIGSTOP and SIGCONT.
concepts.why: Stopping a stuck program correctly, without losing data, depends on picking the right signal.
concepts.body:
A **signal** is a small asynchronous notification the kernel delivers to a process. Programs can **handle** most signals (run cleanup code), **ignore** them, or accept the default action, usually termination. The ones to know:

- `SIGTERM` (15): "please terminate". The default of `kill`; well-behaved programs save state and exit. systemd and Docker send it first when stopping.
- `SIGINT` (2): what Ctrl-C sends to the foreground process.
- `SIGKILL` (9): terminates immediately. It **cannot be caught**, so no cleanup happens: temporary files, locks and half-written data may remain. Use it only when SIGTERM fails.
- `SIGHUP` (1): originally "terminal hung up"; many daemons (nginx, sshd) reload their configuration on it.
- `SIGSTOP` / `SIGCONT`: pause and resume (Ctrl-Z sends the catchable `SIGTSTP`).
- `SIGCHLD`, `SIGPIPE`, `SIGSEGV` happen automatically.

Send them with `kill -SIGNAL PID` (`kill -TERM 1234`, `kill -9 1234`), by name with `pkill pattern` or `killall name`, and list them with `kill -l`. You can only signal your own processes unless you are root.

The usual escalation: `kill PID`, wait a few seconds, check with `ps`, and only then `kill -9`. A process in state `D` or a zombie will not die from signals at all: fix the I/O problem or the parent.
concepts.code:
sleep 600 &
pid=$!
kill "$pid"                          # SIGTERM (15): please exit
sleep 600 & pid=$!
kill -STOP "$pid"
ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p "$pid"         # STAT T = stopped
kill -CONT "$pid"                    # resume
kill -9 "$pid"                       # SIGKILL: no cleanup, last resort
kill -l | head -n 2                  # signal numbers and names
pkill -f 'python worker.py'          # match against full command lines
sudo kill -HUP "$(pgrep -o nginx)"   # nginx reloads its config on SIGHUP
sudo systemctl kill -s HUP nginx     # same, for a systemd service
takeaways: kill sends SIGTERM by default: ask first
SIGKILL (9) cannot be handled; use it last
SIGHUP often means 'reload configuration'
pitfalls: Reaching for kill -9 first, losing the program's chance to flush data and remove lock files.

quiz.q: Which signal can a program NOT catch or ignore?
quiz.explain: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) are handled by the kernel; the process gets no chance to react.

quiz.q: What does Ctrl-C send to the foreground process?
quiz.explain: The terminal driver turns Ctrl-C into SIGINT.

concepts.name: Installing software with package managers
concepts.summary: Install, update, search and remove software with apt on Debian/Ubuntu and dnf on Fedora/RHEL.
concepts.why: Package managers install software with dependencies and security updates; manual installs rot.
concepts.body:
Distributions ship software as **packages** from signed **repositories**. The package manager resolves dependencies, installs files, records what owns each file and later upgrades everything together, including security fixes. That is why the first answer to "how do I install X" should be the package manager.

On **Debian and Ubuntu** (`apt`, `.deb`):

- `sudo apt update` refreshes the package lists (do this first),
- `sudo apt install pkg`, `sudo apt remove pkg` (`purge` also deletes config), `sudo apt upgrade`,
- `apt search term`, `apt show pkg`, `dpkg -L pkg` lists a package's files, `dpkg -S /path` finds the owner of a file.

On **Fedora, RHEL, Rocky and Alma** (`dnf`, `.rpm`): `sudo dnf install pkg`, `dnf remove`, `dnf upgrade`, `dnf search`, `dnf provides /usr/bin/dig` and `rpm -ql pkg`. Others: `pacman -S` on Arch, `apk add` on Alpine, `zypper` on SUSE.

Extra repositories (PPAs, EPEL, vendor repos for Docker or PostgreSQL) add software the distribution does not carry; only add sources you trust, since packages install as root. Universal formats like **Snap** and **Flatpak** bundle dependencies for desktop apps. Language package managers (`pip`, `npm`) should not write into system directories: use virtual environments or per-user installs.
concepts.code:
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt update                  # refresh package lists first
sudo apt install -y htop         # install with dependencies
apt search ripgrep               # find packages
apt show nginx | head -n 5       # version, size, description
sudo apt upgrade                 # update everything installed
sudo apt remove htop             # purge would also delete its config
dpkg -L curl | head -n 3         # files installed by a package
dpkg -S /usr/bin/ssh             # openssh-client: /usr/bin/ssh
# Fedora / RHEL
sudo dnf install htop
dnf provides /usr/bin/dig        # which package ships a file
# Arch: sudo pacman -S htop     Alpine: apk add htop
takeaways: apt update before apt install; dnf on the RPM side
dpkg -S / dnf provides find which package owns a file
Prefer distribution packages; add only trusted repositories
pitfalls: Installing with `sudo pip install` into the system Python and breaking OS tools.

quiz.q: On Ubuntu, `apt install foo` says 'Unable to locate package' for a package that exists. What should you try first?
quiz.explain: The local package lists may be outdated or empty, for example in a fresh container.

quiz.q: How do you find which package provides /usr/bin/dig on Fedora?
quiz.explain: dnf provides searches package file lists for the given path.

concepts.name: Disk and memory usage: df, du, free
concepts.summary: Check free disk space with df, find what uses it with du, and read memory usage correctly with free.
concepts.why: Full disks and memory pressure are among the most frequent causes of outages.
concepts.body:
`df -h` shows each mounted filesystem's size, used and available space in human-readable units. `df -h /var` shows just the filesystem that holds `/var`. A filesystem can also run out of **inodes** (one per file) while bytes are still free, typically with millions of tiny files; check with `df -i`.

`du` measures what directories contain: `du -sh dir` gives one total, and `du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h` lists subdirectories by size so you can drill down. `ncdu` is an interactive alternative. If `df` reports a full disk but `du` cannot find the space, a process may still hold a **deleted** file open (often a rotated log); `lsof +L1` lists such files, and restarting the process frees the space.

`free -h` shows memory. Linux deliberately uses spare RAM as **page cache** for files, so "free" is often small on a healthy machine. The number that matters is **available**: memory that can be handed to programs, including reclaimable cache. **Swap** is disk space used as overflow; some swap use is fine, but constant swapping in and out makes everything slow.

On servers, keep an eye on `/var` (logs, databases, Docker images in `/var/lib/docker`) and set up log rotation and monitoring before the disk fills.
concepts.code:
df -h                          # free space per mounted filesystem
df -h /var                     # only the filesystem holding /var
df -i /                        # inode usage: "No space left" with free bytes?
du -sh ~/Downloads             # total size of one directory
sudo du -h --max-depth=1 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -n 5   # biggest subdirs
sudo lsof +L1                  # deleted files still held open
free -h
#        total   used   free  shared  buff/cache  available
# Mem:    15Gi  4.1Gi  1.0Gi   0.5Gi        10Gi       10Gi
# Swap:  2.0Gi     0B  2.0Gi
takeaways: df shows free space per filesystem, du shows what uses it
df -i for inodes; lsof +L1 for deleted-but-open files
In free, read 'available', not 'free'
pitfalls: Panicking because `free` shows little free memory, when most of it is reclaimable page cache.

quiz.q: df says the disk is 100% full but du on / totals much less. A likely cause?
options: A process holds a deleted file open
quiz.explain: Space of a deleted file is freed only when the last process closes it; lsof +L1 finds them.

quiz.q: Which column of `free -h` best tells you how much memory new programs can use?
quiz.explain: available includes page cache that the kernel can reclaim on demand.

concepts.name: Inodes, hard links and symlinks
concepts.summary: How files really work: inodes hold the data and metadata, names are links to them, and symlinks are paths.
concepts.why: Links explain deployments with a 'current' symlink, why deleting a file may not free space, and many tool behaviours.
concepts.body:
On a Linux filesystem, a file's data and metadata (owner, permissions, size, timestamps) live in an **inode**, identified by a number. A **directory** is just a table mapping names to inode numbers. `ls -i` shows the numbers and `stat` the full metadata.

A **hard link** (`ln target name`) adds another name for the same inode. Both names are equal; there is no "original". The inode keeps a **link count**, and the data is freed only when the count reaches zero **and** no process has the file open. Hard links cannot cross filesystems and cannot point to directories.

A **symbolic link** (`ln -s target name`) is a small special file that contains a **path**. Opening it follows the path. Symlinks can point anywhere, including directories and other filesystems, but if the target is moved or deleted the link **dangles**. A relative target is resolved relative to the link's own directory, not your current one.

Useful commands: `readlink link` prints the stored path, `readlink -f` the fully resolved one; `ls -l` shows `name -> target`; `find -L` follows links, `find -type l` finds them.

A common deployment pattern: install each release in its own directory and atomically switch a `current` symlink with `ln -sfn /opt/app-2.1 /opt/app/current`, making rollbacks instant.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
echo "hello" > original.txt
ln original.txt hard.txt          # hard link: another name, same inode
ln -s original.txt soft.txt       # symlink: a file containing a path
ls -li | sort -k10
# 1234 -rw-r--r-- 2 ada ada  6 ... hard.txt
# 1234 -rw-r--r-- 2 ada ada  6 ... original.txt
# 1240 lrwxrwxrwx 1 ada ada 12 ... soft.txt -> original.txt
rm original.txt
cat hard.txt                      # hello  (data lives while a link remains)
cat soft.txt                      # cat: soft.txt: No such file or directory
readlink soft.txt                 # original.txt  (the dangling path)
stat -c '%h links: %n' hard.txt   # 1 links: hard.txt
mkdir app-2.0 app-2.1
ln -sfn app-2.1 current && readlink current   # app-2.1  (switch a release)
takeaways: An inode holds data and metadata; names are links to it
Hard links share an inode; symlinks store a path and can dangle
ln -sfn atomically repoints a 'current' symlink
pitfalls: Creating a relative symlink from another directory and expecting the path to be relative to where you ran ln.

quiz.q: After `ln a.txt b.txt; rm a.txt`, what happens to b.txt?
options: It still has the full content
quiz.explain: Both names pointed to the same inode; removing one name leaves the data reachable through the other.

quiz.q: Which can point to a directory on another filesystem?
quiz.explain: Symlinks store a path, so they can point anywhere; hard links stay within one filesystem and not at directories.

concepts.name: umask, setuid, setgid and sticky bit
concepts.summary: Default permissions via umask, and the special bits that make passwd work, shared group folders and a safe /tmp.
concepts.why: These bits explain permissions you will see on real systems and are essential for shared directories and security audits.
concepts.body:
New files are created with mode 666 and directories with 777, minus the bits in your **umask**. The common umask `022` removes write for group and others, giving `644` files and `755` directories; `077` makes everything private. Set it in a shell profile, or per service with systemd's `UMask=`.

Three special bits form a fourth, leading octal digit:

- **setuid** (4000, `s` in the user triplet): an executable runs with its **owner's** privileges. `/usr/bin/passwd` is setuid root so ordinary users can update `/etc/shadow`. Setuid programs are prime attack targets; audit them with `find / -perm -4000`.
- **setgid** (2000, `s` in the group triplet): on a **directory**, new files inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group, which is ideal for team folders. On executables it runs with the file's group.
- **sticky bit** (1000, `t` in the others triplet): on a directory, users may delete only their **own** files even if the directory is world-writable. That is why `/tmp` is `1777`.

A capital `S` or `T` means the special bit is set without the underlying execute bit.

When owner/group/other is not expressive enough, **ACLs** (`setfacl -m u:bob:rw file`, `getfacl`) grant permissions to additional users and groups; a `+` after the mode in `ls -l` signals an ACL.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
umask                            # 0022 -> new files 644, directories 755
(umask 077; touch private.txt; stat -c '%a %n' private.txt)   # 600 private.txt
ls -l /usr/bin/passwd            # -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ...  (setuid root)
ls -ld /tmp                      # drwxrwxrwt ...  (sticky)
mkdir team && chmod 2775 team
stat -c '%A %a' team             # drwxrwsr-x 2775  (setgid directory)
chmod +t team && stat -c '%a' team   # 3775
find /usr/bin -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | head -n 3   # setuid binaries
# sudo setfacl -m u:bob:rw report.txt && getfacl report.txt  # per-user ACL
takeaways: umask subtracts bits from 666/777 for new files and directories
setuid runs as the file owner; setgid dirs share a group; sticky protects others' files
ACLs grant extra users or groups access
pitfalls: Setting setuid on a shell script or an interpreter, which opens an easy privilege escalation.

quiz.q: Why is /tmp mode 1777?
options: Everyone can create files, but only owners can delete their own
So only root can write there
New files inherit the tmp group
quiz.explain: The sticky bit (1) on a world-writable directory protects each user's files from others.

quiz.q: With umask 027, what mode does a new regular file get?
quiz.explain: 666 with group write and all 'other' bits removed gives 640.

concepts.name: Managing users and sudo rules
concepts.summary: Create and modify users and groups, grant sudo rights with drop-in files, and lock or remove accounts.
concepts.why: Onboarding people, creating service accounts and limiting admin rights are routine server tasks.
concepts.body:
The low-level tools work on every distribution:

- `useradd -m -s /bin/bash name` creates a user with a home directory and shell (Debian's friendlier `adduser` asks interactively),
- `passwd name` sets a password, `passwd -l name` locks it,
- `usermod -aG group name` **adds** a supplementary group. Without `-a`, `-G` replaces all supplementary groups, a classic way to remove someone's sudo rights by accident,
- `groupadd`, `gpasswd -d user group` (remove from a group), `userdel -r name` (also delete the home).

Group changes take effect at the user's **next login** (or with `newgrp group` in a single shell), since group membership is fixed when a session starts.

**Service accounts** for daemons are system users without a login shell: `useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin myapp`.

**sudo rules** live in `/etc/sudoers`. Never edit it directly: `visudo` checks the syntax, because a broken sudoers file can lock everyone out of root. Prefer small files in `/etc/sudoers.d/`, edited with `visudo -f`. A rule reads `who where=(as_whom) what`; for automation grant exact commands, optionally with `NOPASSWD`, rather than `ALL`. For people, SSH key logins plus sudo are the norm, and direct root login over SSH is disabled.
concepts.code:
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "Bob Builder" bob   # -m creates /home/bob
sudo passwd bob                    # set a password
sudo usermod -aG docker bob        # ADD to a group (-a is essential!)
groups bob                         # bob : bob docker
sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin myapp
sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy
#   deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp
sudo -u postgres psql              # run a command as another user
sudo passwd -l bob                 # lock the password
sudo userdel -r bob                # delete user and home directory
takeaways: usermod -aG adds a group; without -a you replace them all
Group changes apply at the next login
Edit sudo rules with visudo, in /etc/sudoers.d, granting exact commands
pitfalls: `usermod -G docker bob` without -a, silently removing bob from sudo and every other group.

quiz.q: Why use visudo instead of editing /etc/sudoers with any editor?
options: It is the only editor root has
It validates the syntax so a mistake cannot break sudo
quiz.explain: A syntax error in sudoers can make sudo unusable; visudo refuses to save invalid files.

quiz.q: You added alice to the docker group, but `docker ps` still says permission denied in her open session. Why?
options: Groups are applied at login, so she must log in again or use newgrp
quiz.explain: A session's group list is set at login; new memberships appear in new sessions.

concepts.name: Services with systemctl
concepts.summary: Start, stop, restart, reload, enable and inspect services with systemd's systemctl.
concepts.why: Nearly every server program runs as a systemd service, so systemctl is how you operate them.
concepts.body:
**systemd** is PID 1 on almost all modern distributions. It starts and supervises **units**: services (`.service`), timers, mounts, sockets and targets (groups of units, like `multi-user.target`). You control them with `systemctl`:

- `systemctl status name` shows whether it is running, its main PID, memory, cgroup and the latest log lines: the first command to run when something is wrong,
- `start`, `stop`, `restart`, and `reload` (re-read configuration without a restart, if the service supports it),
- `enable` makes it start at boot, `disable` stops that; `enable --now` does both enable and start,
- `is-active`, `is-enabled` and `is-failed` give script-friendly answers,
- `systemctl --failed` (or `list-units --state=failed`) lists broken units,
- `systemctl cat name` shows the unit file and its overrides, `systemctl show name` every property.

Note the difference between **running now** (start/stop) and **starting at boot** (enable/disable); forgetting to enable is a classic "worked until the reboot" bug. `mask` prevents a unit from being started at all.

State-changing commands need `sudo`. Users can also run their own services with `systemctl --user`. Services log to the journal, which `journalctl -u name` reads.
concepts.code:
systemctl status nginx              # state, PID, memory, recent log lines
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl stop nginx
sudo systemctl restart nginx        # stop + start
sudo systemctl reload nginx         # re-read config, keep connections
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx   # start at boot AND right now
systemctl is-active nginx           # active
systemctl is-enabled nginx          # enabled
systemctl --failed                  # units that failed
systemctl cat nginx                 # the unit file and overrides
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running | head
systemctl --user status syncthing   # a per-user service
takeaways: status first; start/stop/restart/reload for now, enable/disable for boot
enable --now does both
systemctl --failed shows what is broken
pitfalls: Starting a service but never enabling it, so it is gone after the next reboot.

quiz.q: Which command makes a service start at boot and also starts it immediately?
quiz.explain: enable creates the boot-time links and --now also starts it.

quiz.q: What is `systemctl reload` for?
options: Re-reading unit files after editing them
Telling the service to re-read its configuration without a full restart
quiz.explain: reload asks the service itself to reload config; daemon-reload is what re-reads unit files.

concepts.name: Logs with journalctl
concepts.summary: Query the systemd journal by unit, time, priority and boot, follow logs live, and manage journal size.
concepts.why: When a service misbehaves, its logs are the first place to look, and journalctl finds them fast.
concepts.body:
systemd's **journal** collects stdout/stderr of every service, kernel messages and syslog messages into one indexed store. `journalctl` queries it, and filters combine:

- `-u nginx` one unit (repeat `-u` for several), `-k` kernel messages only,
- `-f` follow live, `-n 50` the last 50 entries, `-e` jump to the end,
- `--since "1 hour ago"`, `--since today`, `--until "2026-10-01 12:00"`,
- `-p err` priority error and worse (emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug),
- `-b` this boot, `-b -1` the previous boot, `--list-boots` all of them,
- field matches such as `_PID=1234` or `_UID=1000`, and `-o json-pretty` to see all fields.

Output goes through a pager; add `--no-pager` in scripts and pipe to `grep` as usual. Without `sudo` (or membership in `adm` / `systemd-journal`) you see only your own user's logs.

Whether logs survive a reboot depends on **persistent storage**: if `/var/log/journal` exists they do, otherwise they live in `/run` and vanish. Size limits are set in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`; check usage with `--disk-usage` and trim with `--vacuum-size` or `--vacuum-time`.

Many applications (nginx, PostgreSQL) also or instead write classic text logs under `/var/log`, rotated by **logrotate**; read those with `less`, `tail -f` and `grep`.
concepts.code:
journalctl -u nginx                     # one unit's logs
journalctl -u nginx -f                  # follow live
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager | grep -i error
journalctl -p err -b                    # errors and worse, this boot
journalctl -b -1 -e                     # previous boot, jump to the end
journalctl -k -n 20                     # last 20 kernel messages
journalctl _PID=1234                    # by field
journalctl -u nginx -o json-pretty -n 1 # every field of one entry
journalctl --disk-usage
sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=2weeks    # drop older entries
sudo tail -F /var/log/nginx/error.log   # classic log files
takeaways: journalctl -u unit -f --since ... -p err -b filter and follow
-b -1 reads the previous boot (with persistent storage)
Many apps also write text logs in /var/log, rotated by logrotate
pitfalls: Looking for logs from before a crash-reboot when the journal is not persistent.

quiz.q: How do you see errors from the boot before the current one?
quiz.explain: -b -1 selects the previous boot and -p err filters by priority.

quiz.q: journalctl shows only a few lines for a system service when run without sudo. Why?
options: Unprivileged users only see their own logs unless in adm/systemd-journal
quiz.explain: System logs require root or membership in a log-reading group.

concepts.name: Scheduling: cron and systemd timers
concepts.summary: Run jobs on a schedule with crontab syntax or systemd timers, and avoid the environment pitfalls.
concepts.why: Backups, cleanups and reports all need to run reliably on a schedule without anyone logged in.
concepts.body:
**cron** runs commands at times given by five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, followed by the command. `*` means every value, `*/5` every fifth, `1-5` a range, `1,15` a list. So `30 2 * * *` is 02:30 daily and `*/10 * * * 1-5` every ten minutes on weekdays. Edit your own table with `crontab -e`, list it with `crontab -l`; system jobs go in `/etc/cron.d/` with an extra user field.

Cron jobs run with a **minimal environment**: a short `PATH`, no shell profile, the home directory as working directory. Use absolute paths, set variables at the top of the crontab or in the script, and **redirect output** (`>> log 2>&1`) or it is mailed to a mailbox nobody reads. Remember that `%` has a special meaning in crontab lines and must be escaped as `\%`.

**systemd timers** are the modern alternative: a `.timer` unit triggers a `.service` unit. Benefits: output goes to the journal, `Persistent=true` runs missed jobs after downtime, `RandomizedDelaySec=` spreads load, resource limits and dependencies apply, and `systemctl list-timers` shows next and last runs. `OnCalendar=` uses expressions like `daily`, `Mon..Fri 09:00` or `*-*-* 02:30:00`; check them with `systemd-analyze calendar`. For a one-off delayed command, `systemd-run --on-active=30m cmd` or `at` work.
concepts.code:
crontab -e                         # edit YOUR crontab, lines like:
#   m    h  dom mon dow  command
#   30   2  *   *   *    /home/ada/bin/backup.sh >> /home/ada/backup.log 2>&1
#   */10 *  *   *   1-5  /usr/local/bin/check-queue
crontab -l                         # list it
# systemd alternative: /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer
#   [Timer]
#   OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
#   Persistent=true                # catch up if the machine was off
#   [Install]
#   WantedBy=timers.target
# ...plus backup.service with ExecStart=/home/ada/bin/backup.sh
sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer
systemctl list-timers              # next and last run of every timer
systemd-analyze calendar 'Mon..Fri 09:00'   # when does this fire next?
takeaways: Five cron fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week
Cron has a minimal environment: absolute paths and redirect output
systemd timers add logging, catch-up runs and list-timers
pitfalls: A script that works in your terminal but fails in cron because PATH or variables are missing.

quiz.q: What does the cron schedule `0 */6 * * *` mean?
quiz.explain: Minute 0, every sixth hour: 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00.

quiz.q: Which systemd timer option runs a missed job after the machine was powered off at the scheduled time?
quiz.explain: Persistent=true records the last run and triggers immediately if a run was missed.

concepts.name: Networking tools: ip, ss, dig, curl
concepts.summary: Inspect interfaces, routes, listening ports and DNS, and test connectivity layer by layer.
concepts.why: Most 'the service is down' tickets are network questions you can answer with five commands.
concepts.body:
Debug network problems **layer by layer**, from the interface up to the application:

- **Interfaces and addresses**: `ip addr` (`ip -br a` for a brief view) shows interfaces, their state and IPs; `ip link` the link layer. The old `ifconfig` is deprecated.
- **Routes**: `ip route` shows the routing table; the `default via` line is your gateway. `ip route get 8.8.8.8` tells which route and source address a destination would use.
- **Reachability**: `ping -c 3 host` (ICMP may be blocked by firewalls), `tracepath` or `mtr` for the path.
- **DNS**: `dig +short name` or `getent hosts name` (which also honours `/etc/hosts`); resolvers are listed in `/etc/resolv.conf`, often pointing at the local `systemd-resolved` (check `resolvectl status`).
- **Ports**: `ss -tlnp` lists listening TCP sockets with the owning process (run with sudo to see all), `ss -tnp` current connections. A service bound to `127.0.0.1` is reachable only from the machine itself; `0.0.0.0` or `[::]` means all interfaces.
- **Application**: `curl -v https://host/path` shows the TLS handshake, request and response headers; `nc -zv host 5432` tests whether a TCP port accepts connections.

Network configuration itself is distribution-specific: netplan on Ubuntu, NetworkManager (`nmcli`) on Fedora/RHEL and desktops, systemd-networkd elsewhere.
concepts.code:
ip -br addr                   # interfaces and addresses
# lo    UNKNOWN  127.0.0.1/8 ::1/128
# eth0  UP       192.168.1.20/24 fe80::1c2:3ff:fe4d:5e6f/64
ip route                      # default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 ...
ip route get 1.1.1.1          # which interface and source address would be used
ping -c 3 example.com         # reachability and latency
dig +short example.com        # DNS answer only
getent hosts db.internal      # resolve like applications do (incl. /etc/hosts)
sudo ss -tlnp                 # listening TCP ports with processes
# LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("nginx",pid=812,fd=6))
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' https://example.com
nc -zv db.internal 5432       # is the TCP port open?
takeaways: Check interface, route, DNS, port, then application
ss -tlnp shows what listens where; 127.0.0.1 means local only
dig / getent for DNS, curl -v and nc -zv for services
pitfalls: Concluding a host is down because ping fails, when ICMP is simply blocked.

quiz.q: A web app works with curl on the server but not from other machines. ss shows it listening on 127.0.0.1:8080. Why?
options: It is bound to the loopback interface only
quiz.explain: Loopback addresses accept connections only from the machine itself; bind to 0.0.0.0 or a public interface.

quiz.q: Which command shows listening TCP ports and the processes that own them?
quiz.explain: ss: -t TCP, -l listening, -n numeric, -p process.

concepts.name: Archives and compression: tar, gzip, zstd
concepts.summary: Bundle directories with tar, compress with gzip, xz or zstd, and list or extract archives safely.
concepts.why: Backups, releases and file transfers are almost always tarballs.
concepts.body:
**tar** bundles files and directories, with permissions and timestamps, into one archive; a compressor then shrinks it. The flags read like a sentence:

- `c` create, `x` extract, `t` list the contents,
- `f file` the archive file name (put it last in the flag group),
- `z` gzip, `J` xz, `--zstd` zstd, or `a` to choose by the file extension,
- `v` verbose, `-C dir` change into a directory first.

So `tar -czf backup.tar.gz dir/` creates, `tar -tzf backup.tar.gz` lists, and `tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C /restore` extracts into a directory. Modern GNU tar detects compression automatically on extraction, so `tar -xf` is usually enough. **List before extracting** archives from elsewhere: some contain absolute paths or a pile of files without a top-level directory.

Compressors trade speed for size: **gzip** is universal, **xz** is small but slow, **zstd** is fast with a good ratio and has become the modern default for many projects. Single files can be compressed directly: `gzip file` replaces it with `file.gz` (`-k` keeps the original), `gunzip` or `zcat` reverse it.

`zip` and `unzip` handle the format common on Windows. For copying directories between machines, `rsync -a` or `tar` piped through `ssh` preserve metadata.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)" mkdir -p site/css && echo '

hi

' > site/index.html && echo 'body{}' > site/css/a.css tar -czf site.tar.gz site/ # c=create z=gzip f=file tar -tzf site.tar.gz | sort # t=list: site/ site/css/ site/css/a.css site/index.html mkdir restore && tar -xf site.tar.gz -C restore # x=extract (compression auto-detected) ls restore/site # css index.html tar -caf site.tar.xz site/ # -a: compression chosen from the extension echo 'log line' > app.log gzip app.log && ls app.log* # app.log.gz (original replaced) zcat app.log.gz # log line gunzip app.log.gz && ls app.log* # app.log # tar -cf - site/ | ssh backup 'tar -xf - -C /srv' # copy a tree over ssh
takeaways: tar -czf create, -tzf list, -xf extract, -C target directory
gzip is universal, zstd fast, xz small
List untrusted archives before extracting them
pitfalls: Extracting an unknown archive in your home directory and getting hundreds of loose files.

quiz.q: Which command lists the contents of backup.tar.gz without extracting?
quiz.explain: t lists, x extracts, c creates.

quiz.q: What happens to app.log after `gzip app.log`?
options: It is kept next to app.log.gz
quiz.explain: gzip replaces the file with its compressed version unless -k is given.

concepts.name: Block devices, filesystems and mounts
concepts.summary: Identify disks with lsblk, create filesystems, mount them by UUID and make mounts permanent with fstab.
concepts.why: Adding a volume to a server or recovering a non-booting one requires understanding how disks become directories.
concepts.body:
Disks appear as **block devices** in `/dev`: `/dev/sda`, `/dev/nvme0n1`, `/dev/vdb` in VMs, with partitions such as `/dev/sda1` or `/dev/nvme0n1p1`. `lsblk -f` shows the whole tree with filesystem types, labels, UUIDs and mount points; `blkid` prints UUIDs.

A partition or volume must hold a **filesystem** before use: `mkfs.ext4` or `mkfs.xfs` create one (and destroy what was there). **ext4** is the solid default, **XFS** is the RHEL default and handles large files well but cannot shrink, **Btrfs** offers snapshots and checksums.

**Mounting** attaches a filesystem to a directory: `mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data`; `umount` detaches it. "target is busy" means a process still uses it (check with `lsof` or `fuser -vm`). `findmnt` shows what is mounted where, with options.

To mount at boot, add a line to `/etc/fstab`: device, mount point, type, options, dump, fsck order. Always refer to the device by **UUID** (or label), since `/dev/sdX` names can change between boots. Useful options: `defaults`, `noatime`, `ro`, and **`nofail`** for non-essential disks so a missing disk does not stop the boot. Test with `findmnt --verify` and `mount -a` before rebooting; a bad fstab can drop the machine into emergency mode.

Special filesystems need no disk: `tmpfs` lives in RAM, and network filesystems (NFS, SMB) mount remote shares.
concepts.code:
lsblk -f                            # devices, filesystems, UUIDs, mount points
findmnt /                           # what is mounted at /, with options
sudo mkfs.ext4 -L data /dev/sdb1    # new filesystem (DESTROYS existing data)
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data
sudo blkid /dev/sdb1                # UUID="3f1c..." TYPE="ext4" LABEL="data"
# /etc/fstab  (by UUID, never /dev/sdX):
# UUID=3f1c...  /mnt/data  ext4  defaults,noatime,nofail  0  2
sudo findmnt --verify               # check fstab before rebooting
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo mount -a   # mount everything listed
sudo umount /mnt/data               # "target is busy"? -> sudo fuser -vm /mnt/data
sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=1G tmpfs /mnt/scratch   # RAM-backed filesystem
takeaways: lsblk -f and blkid identify devices, filesystems and UUIDs
mkfs creates a filesystem; mount attaches it to a directory
fstab by UUID with nofail; verify before rebooting
pitfalls: Using /dev/sdb1 in fstab, then a new disk shifts the names and the wrong device (or none) is mounted.

quiz.q: Why should /etc/fstab refer to filesystems by UUID?
options: Device names like /dev/sdb can change between boots
quiz.explain: Kernel device naming depends on detection order; the UUID is stored in the filesystem itself.

quiz.q: What does the `nofail` mount option do?
options: Makes the filesystem read-only on errors
Lets the system boot even if that device is missing
quiz.explain: Without nofail a missing device listed in fstab can block boot.

concepts.name: Partitions and LVM
concepts.summary: Partition disks with GPT, and pool them with LVM to resize volumes online and take snapshots.
concepts.why: Growing a full volume without downtime is a routine but nerve-wracking task unless you know LVM.
concepts.body:
A disk is divided into **partitions** described by a partition table. **GPT** is the modern standard (large disks, many partitions, required for UEFI boot); the older **MBR** is limited to 2 TiB. Create partitions with `fdisk`, `gdisk` or scriptable `parted`, then let the kernel re-read the table (`partprobe`).

**LVM** (Logical Volume Manager) adds a flexible layer between disks and filesystems:

- **physical volumes** (PV): disks or partitions initialised with `pvcreate`,
- a **volume group** (VG): a pool built from one or more PVs with `vgcreate`,
- **logical volumes** (LV): virtual block devices carved from the pool with `lvcreate`, used like partitions at `/dev/vgname/lvname`.

The payoff: when a volume fills up, add a disk to the VG (`vgextend`) and grow the LV **while mounted** with `lvextend -r`, where `-r` also resizes the filesystem. ext4 and XFS can grow online; only ext4 can shrink, and only unmounted. `pvs`, `vgs` and `lvs` summarise the layout.

**Snapshots** (`lvcreate -s`) freeze a point-in-time view, handy before an upgrade or for consistent backups; they consume space as the origin changes, so remove them afterwards.

In the cloud you often grow the disk itself: resize it in the provider, then `growpart` the partition and resize the PV or filesystem. Always take a backup before touching partition tables.
concepts.code:
sudo fdisk -l /dev/sdb                    # current partition table
sudo parted /dev/sdb --script mklabel gpt mkpart data 1MiB 100%
# LVM: physical volumes -> volume group -> logical volumes
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
sudo vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
sudo lvcreate -n lvapp -L 50G vgdata
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/lvapp
sudo pvs; sudo vgs; sudo lvs              # summaries
# Out of space? Add a disk and grow online:
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdd1 && sudo vgextend vgdata /dev/sdd1
sudo lvextend -r -L +20G /dev/vgdata/lvapp   # -r grows the filesystem too
sudo lvcreate -s -n before-upgrade -L 5G /dev/vgdata/lvapp   # snapshot
# Cloud disk resized in the console instead:
sudo growpart /dev/nvme0n1 1 && sudo resize2fs /dev/nvme0n1p1   # (xfs_growfs for XFS)
takeaways: GPT partition tables; MBR only for legacy
LVM: PV -> VG -> LV, grow online with lvextend -r
Snapshots before risky changes; remove them afterwards
pitfalls: Extending the logical volume but forgetting to grow the filesystem, so df shows no change.

quiz.q: You ran `lvextend -L +20G /dev/vg/lv` and df still shows the old size. What is missing?
options: Growing the filesystem (resize2fs / xfs_growfs, or use lvextend -r)
quiz.explain: The block device grew but the filesystem on it must be resized too.

quiz.q: What is a volume group in LVM?
options: A pool of storage made of physical volumes, from which logical volumes are allocated
quiz.explain: VGs aggregate PVs; LVs are carved out of the VG.

concepts.name: /proc, /sys and sysctl
concepts.summary: Read process and system information straight from /proc and /sys, and tune kernel parameters with sysctl.
concepts.why: Tools like ps, top and free are just readers of /proc; going direct answers questions they cannot.
concepts.body:
`/proc` is a virtual filesystem where the kernel publishes live information as text files. Nothing is stored on disk; each read is generated on demand.

System-wide files: `/proc/cpuinfo`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/loadavg`, `/proc/uptime`, `/proc/mounts`, `/proc/cmdline` (kernel boot parameters) and `/proc/pressure/*` (pressure stall information: how long tasks waited for CPU, memory or I/O).

Per-process directories `/proc/<PID>/` (and `/proc/self` for the reader):

- `cmdline` (arguments separated by NUL bytes), `environ`, `cwd` and `exe` (symlinks),
- `status` (state, memory such as `VmRSS`, threads, UIDs), `limits` (ulimits),
- `fd/` (one symlink per open file descriptor, including sockets), `cgroup`, `ns/` (namespaces).

`/sys` (sysfs) exposes the device and driver model: network interfaces in `/sys/class/net`, block devices in `/sys/block`, CPU frequency, power settings and the cgroup tree in `/sys/fs/cgroup`.

**Kernel tunables** live in `/proc/sys` and are managed with `sysctl`: `sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward` reads one, `sysctl -w` changes it until reboot, and files in `/etc/sysctl.d/*.conf` make settings permanent (`sysctl --system` applies them). Common examples: enabling IP forwarding for routers and containers, `vm.swappiness`, `fs.inotify.max_user_watches` for file watchers, and network buffer sizes. Change tunables deliberately and document why.
concepts.code:
grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo
grep -E 'MemTotal|MemAvailable' /proc/meminfo
cat /proc/loadavg                       # 0.15 0.10 0.05 1/312 4567
tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/$$/cmdline; echo    # this shell's command line
readlink /proc/$$/cwd                   # its working directory
grep -E '^(State|VmRSS|Threads)' /proc/$$/status
ls -l /proc/$$/fd | tail -n +2 | head -n 3   # open file descriptors
cat /sys/class/net/lo/mtu               # 65536
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward       # 0 or 1, same as: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
# sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10                                  # until reboot
# echo 'vm.swappiness = 10' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-local.conf # permanent
# sudo sysctl --system                                             # apply all files
takeaways: /proc/<PID>/ holds cmdline, status, fd, cwd and more for each process
/sys exposes devices, drivers and cgroups
sysctl -w for now, /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf for permanent
pitfalls: Changing a tunable with sysctl -w and losing it at the next reboot.

quiz.q: Where can you see every file and socket a process with PID 812 has open?
quiz.explain: /proc/<PID>/fd contains one symlink per open file descriptor.

quiz.q: How do you make a sysctl setting survive reboots?
options: Write it to a file in /etc/sysctl.d/
quiz.explain: Files in /etc/sysctl.d are applied at boot; sysctl -w and /proc/sys writes are temporary.

concepts.name: Firewalls: nftables, ufw and firewalld
concepts.summary: Filter incoming traffic with ufw or firewalld, and understand the nftables rules underneath.
concepts.why: A default-deny firewall that allows only the services you run is basic server hygiene.
concepts.body:
The kernel's packet filter is **netfilter**, configured today with **nftables** (`nft`), the successor to iptables. On most iptables-using systems the `iptables` command is a compatibility layer over nftables. Distributions add friendlier front ends:

- **ufw** on Ubuntu: `ufw allow 443/tcp`, `ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 5432`, `ufw enable`, `ufw status numbered`,
- **firewalld** on Fedora/RHEL: **zones** with services, `firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent` followed by `--reload`.

Use one front end per machine; mixing them produces confusing, overlapping rules.

The typical policy for a server's **input** chain: drop by default, accept packets of **established/related** connections (replies to traffic you started), accept the loopback interface, accept the specific ports you serve, and accept ICMP. With IPv6, ICMPv6 is essential: neighbour discovery breaks without it.

Before enabling a default-drop policy over SSH, **allow SSH first**, and keep a second session open or use a timed rollback; locking yourself out of a remote machine is a rite of passage best avoided.

Remember that cloud environments add security groups in front of the host, and Docker inserts its own rules for published ports, which can bypass ufw. Check what really happens with `nft list ruleset`.
concepts.code:
# Ubuntu: ufw
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH            # FIRST, or you lock yourself out
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 5432 proto tcp
sudo ufw enable && sudo ufw status verbose
# Fedora / RHEL: firewalld
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent && sudo firewall-cmd --reload
# nftables directly, /etc/nftables.conf:
# table inet filter {
#   chain input {
#     type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
#     ct state established,related accept
#     iif lo accept
#     meta l4proto { icmp, ipv6-icmp } accept
#     tcp dport { 22, 443 } accept
#   }
# }
sudo nft -c -f /etc/nftables.conf && sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf   # check, then load
sudo nft list ruleset             # what is really active
takeaways: nftables is the kernel firewall; ufw and firewalld are front ends
Default drop, allow established, loopback, ICMP and your ports
Allow SSH before enabling a firewall remotely
pitfalls: Enabling a default-deny firewall over SSH without allowing port 22 first.

quiz.q: Why does a server firewall accept `ct state established,related` packets?
options: So replies to connections the server started (and existing sessions) get through
It is required by ufw only
quiz.explain: Connection tracking lets return traffic in without opening ports for new inbound connections.

quiz.q: Which statement about Docker and ufw is true?
options: Docker's own rules for published ports can bypass ufw
Docker requires ufw to be disabled
quiz.explain: Docker inserts rules that handle published ports before ufw's rules see the traffic.

concepts.name: Troubleshooting performance
concepts.summary: Diagnose a slow machine methodically: load, CPU, memory, swap, disk I/O and the OOM killer.
concepts.why: When production is slow, a calm checklist beats guessing and restarting things.
concepts.body:
Work through resources one at a time; for each, ask about **utilization**, **saturation** (queueing) and **errors**.

- **Load average** (`uptime`, `top`): the average number of tasks running or waiting over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. On Linux it also counts tasks in uninterruptible I/O wait, so compare it with `nproc` and check whether CPU or I/O is the cause.
- **CPU**: `top` or `htop` per process; `mpstat -P ALL 1` per core. High `us` is your code, high `sy` the kernel, high `wa` waiting for I/O, and `st` (steal) means the hypervisor is giving your VM less than you think.
- **Memory**: `free -h` (the available column), `vmstat 1` with `si`/`so` for swapping. When memory runs out, the **OOM killer** terminates a process; `dmesg -T | grep -i oom` or `journalctl -k` show the victims.
- **Disk**: `iostat -xz 1` (sysstat package) shows utilization, queue size and latency (`await`) per device; `iotop` shows which processes do I/O; `df -h` rules out a full disk.
- **Per process**: `pidstat 1`, `/proc/<PID>/status`, `lsof -p` for open files and sockets.
- **Pressure stall information** in `/proc/pressure/{cpu,memory,io}` directly reports the share of time tasks were stalled.

`vmstat 1` is the best single first command: its `r`, `b`, `si/so`, `wa` columns show at a glance which resource is under pressure.
concepts.code:
uptime                      # load average: 3.10, 2.05, 1.20  (1, 5, 15 min)
nproc                       # 4 -> a load above 4 means tasks are queuing
vmstat 1 5                  # r=runnable b=blocked si/so=swap wa=I/O wait st=steal
top -o %MEM                 # or htop; sort processes by memory
free -h                     # look at 'available'
cat /proc/pressure/memory   # some avg10=0.00 ... full avg10=0.00 ...
iostat -xz 1 3              # per-disk %util and await latency (sysstat)
sudo iotop -o               # processes doing I/O right now
pidstat -u 1 5              # per-process CPU over time
sudo dmesg -T | grep -iE 'out of memory|killed process'   # OOM killer victims
sudo lsof -p 1234 | wc -l   # how many files/sockets a process holds
takeaways: Check CPU, memory, disk and network for utilization, saturation and errors
vmstat 1 is the best first command; load counts I/O waits too
dmesg / journalctl -k reveal OOM kills
pitfalls: Adding CPUs to a machine whose high load average is actually caused by tasks waiting on a slow disk.

quiz.q: A 4-core server has load average 12 but CPU is mostly idle and wa is high. What is the likely bottleneck?
quiz.explain: Linux load includes tasks in uninterruptible I/O wait; idle CPU with high wa points at storage.

quiz.q: A process disappeared and the kernel log says 'Out of memory: Killed process 4242'. What happened?
options: The OOM killer terminated it to free memory
The process crashed with a segfault
quiz.explain: When memory is exhausted the kernel's OOM killer picks and kills a process.

concepts.name: Writing systemd unit files
concepts.summary: Turn your own program into a supervised service with a unit file: dependencies, restarts, users, environment and hardening.
concepts.why: A proper unit file gives your app automatic restarts, logging, boot-time start and security sandboxing for free.
concepts.body:
Custom units go in `/etc/systemd/system/name.service`. A service unit has three sections:

- `[Unit]`: `Description=`, and ordering/dependencies such as `After=network-online.target` with `Wants=network-online.target`, or `Requires=postgresql.service`.
- `[Service]`: how to run it. `ExecStart=` needs an absolute path and runs the program **directly**, without a shell, so pipes and `$(...)` do not work unless you call `/bin/sh -c`. `Type=simple` (default: the process stays in the foreground), `notify` (the program signals readiness) or `oneshot` (scripts that exit). Add `User=`, `WorkingDirectory=`, `Environment=` or `EnvironmentFile=`, and `Restart=on-failure` with `RestartSec=5`.
- `[Install]`: `WantedBy=multi-user.target` makes `enable` start it at boot.

After creating or editing a unit run `systemctl daemon-reload`. To change a unit shipped by a package, do not edit it in `/usr/lib/systemd/system`: run `systemctl edit name`, which creates a **drop-in** override in `/etc/systemd/system/name.service.d/`.

systemd can sandbox a service with a few lines: `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `ProtectSystem=strict` (read-only filesystem except `ReadWritePaths=`), `ProtectHome=yes`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, or `DynamicUser=yes` for a throwaway user. `systemd-analyze security name` scores how exposed a service is. The app should log to stdout/stderr and let the journal handle storage.
concepts.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My web app
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=myapp
WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp
EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/env
ExecStart=/opt/myapp/bin/server --port 8080
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/myapp
PrivateTmp=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
# Then: sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now myapp
# Override a packaged unit instead of editing it: sudo systemctl edit nginx
takeaways: [Unit] ordering, [Service] how to run, [Install] when to start
ExecStart runs without a shell; daemon-reload after edits
Use drop-ins via systemctl edit and add sandboxing options
pitfalls: Writing `ExecStart=cd /opt/app && ./server`: there is no shell, so && and cd do not work.

quiz.q: You edited /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service. What must you run before restarting it?
quiz.explain: daemon-reload makes systemd re-read unit files; reload only signals the service.

quiz.q: How should you customise a unit file installed by a package?
options: Create a drop-in with systemctl edit
quiz.explain: Drop-ins in /etc override specific settings and survive package upgrades.

concepts.name: The boot process and kernel modules
concepts.summary: From firmware to login prompt: bootloader, kernel, initramfs, systemd targets, and loading kernel modules.
concepts.why: Fixing a machine that does not boot, or a driver that does not load, requires knowing each stage.
concepts.body:
Booting happens in stages, and each hands control to the next:

- **Firmware** (UEFI, or legacy BIOS) initialises hardware and starts a bootloader from the EFI system partition.
- The **bootloader** (GRUB, or systemd-boot) loads the kernel image and the **initramfs** from `/boot` and passes the **kernel command line** (`/proc/cmdline` shows it afterwards), e.g. `root=UUID=... ro quiet`.
- The **kernel** initialises devices and mounts the initramfs, a small temporary root filesystem holding the drivers and tools needed to find the real root (RAID, LVM, encryption, network root).
- The initramfs mounts the real root filesystem and executes **systemd** as PID 1, which starts units in parallel until the default **target** is reached (`multi-user.target` for servers, `graphical.target` for desktops).

`systemd-analyze`, `blame` and `critical-chain` show where boot time goes. For rescue, edit the kernel line in the bootloader to add `systemd.unit=rescue.target` or `emergency.target`.

Much of the kernel is built as **loadable modules** (drivers, filesystems, netfilter features) in `/lib/modules/$(uname -r)`. `lsmod` lists loaded ones, `modinfo` describes one, `modprobe name` loads it with its dependencies (`-r` removes). Modules usually load automatically when hardware appears; persist manual ones in `/etc/modules-load.d/`, set options in `/etc/modprobe.d/`, and blacklist unwanted drivers there too. After changes that affect early boot, regenerate the initramfs (`update-initramfs -u` or `dracut -f`).
concepts.code:
systemd-analyze                     # Startup finished in 2.1s (kernel) + 6.4s (userspace)
systemd-analyze blame | head -n 5   # slowest units
systemd-analyze critical-chain      # what the boot actually waited for
cat /proc/cmdline                   # BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinuz-6.12... root=UUID=... ro quiet
systemctl get-default               # multi-user.target
uname -r; ls /boot                  # running kernel vs installed kernels and initramfs
lsmod | head -n 5                   # loaded modules, sizes, users
modinfo -F description ext4         # Fourth Extended Filesystem
sudo modprobe br_netfilter          # load a module and its dependencies
echo br_netfilter | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf    # load at every boot
echo 'blacklist nouveau' | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/no-nouveau.conf
sudo update-initramfs -u            # Debian/Ubuntu (dracut -f on Fedora/RHEL)
takeaways: Firmware -> bootloader -> kernel + initramfs -> systemd -> default target
systemd-analyze blame / critical-chain explain slow boots
modprobe loads modules; persist in /etc/modules-load.d, configure in /etc/modprobe.d
pitfalls: Changing storage drivers or encryption setup without regenerating the initramfs, leaving a system that cannot find its root.

quiz.q: What is the initramfs for?
options: A small early root filesystem with the drivers needed to mount the real root
quiz.explain: It lets a generic kernel load storage, LVM or encryption support before the real root exists.

quiz.q: Which file shows the parameters the running kernel was booted with?
quiz.explain: /proc/cmdline reflects what the bootloader actually passed.

concepts.name: Namespaces: how containers isolate
concepts.summary: PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user and cgroup namespaces, explored with unshare, nsenter and ip netns.
concepts.why: Containers are just processes in namespaces; understanding them demystifies Docker and Kubernetes debugging.
concepts.body:
A **namespace** wraps a global resource so that processes inside see their own isolated instance. Linux has eight kinds:

- **PID**: its own process numbering; the first process is PID 1 inside,
- **network**: own interfaces, IPs, routes, firewall rules and ports,
- **mount**: own view of the mount table, so a container sees its own root filesystem,
- **UTS**: own hostname; **IPC**: own System V IPC and POSIX message queues,
- **user**: own UID/GID mappings, so a process can be root inside and an unprivileged user outside (the basis of rootless containers),
- **cgroup** and **time** namespaces virtualise the cgroup tree view and some clocks.

Every process belongs to one namespace of each kind; `/proc/<PID>/ns/` shows them as links whose numbers identify the namespace, and `lsns` lists them system-wide.

`unshare` starts a program in new namespaces (`--pid --fork --mount-proc`, `--net`, `--user --map-root-user`), and `nsenter -t PID -n` (or `-a` for all) runs a command inside another process's namespaces. That is extremely useful for containers: you can use the **host's** tools, such as `ss`, `ip` or `tcpdump`, inside a container's network namespace even if the image has none.

A **container** is roughly: namespaces for isolation, cgroups for resource limits, a layered root filesystem, capabilities and seccomp filters to restrict privileges. There is no "container" object in the kernel.
concepts.code:
ls -l /proc/$$/ns | tail -n +2 | head -n 3   # cgroup, ipc, mnt ... -> 'net:[4026531840]'
sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc ps -o pid,cmd
#   PID CMD
#     1 ps -o pid,cmd       <- new PID namespace: only this process, as PID 1
sudo unshare --net ip -br link              # lo DOWN   (an empty network stack)
unshare --user --map-root-user id -u        # 0  (root inside, no sudo needed)
sudo unshare --uts bash -c 'hostname sandbox; hostname'   # sandbox (host unchanged)
lsns -t net                                 # network namespaces in use
sudo ip netns add blue && sudo ip netns exec blue ip -br link   # lo DOWN
pid=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web)
sudo nsenter -t "$pid" -n ss -tlnp          # host's ss inside the container's netns
takeaways: Namespaces isolate PIDs, network, mounts, hostname, IPC, users, cgroups and time
unshare creates namespaces; nsenter joins a process's namespaces
A container = namespaces + cgroups + root filesystem + restricted privileges
pitfalls: Installing debugging tools inside a running container image instead of entering its namespaces with nsenter.

quiz.q: Which namespace lets an unprivileged user appear as root inside a container?
quiz.explain: The user namespace maps UID 0 inside to an unprivileged UID outside.

quiz.q: How can you run the host's `ss` command inside a container's network namespace?
quiz.explain: nsenter -n joins the target process's network namespace while using the host's binary.

concepts.name: cgroups v2: limiting resources
concepts.summary: Control groups organise processes in a tree and limit their CPU, memory, I/O and process count; systemd and containers use them.
concepts.why: Every memory limit in Docker or Kubernetes, and every systemd resource setting, is a cgroup setting underneath.
concepts.body:
**Control groups** organise processes into a hierarchy and account for and limit their resource use. Modern distributions use the unified **cgroup v2** hierarchy mounted at `/sys/fs/cgroup`. Each cgroup is a directory; its files are the interface:

- `cgroup.procs` lists member PIDs (write a PID to move a process),
- `memory.max` hard memory limit (the OOM killer acts inside the group when exceeded), `memory.high` a throttling threshold, `memory.current` usage,
- `cpu.max` quota and period, for example `50000 100000` for half a CPU; `cpu.weight` a relative share,
- `io.max` per-device bandwidth or IOPS limits, `pids.max` the number of tasks, which stops fork bombs,
- `memory.events`, `cpu.stat` and `*.pressure` files for statistics.

Controllers must be enabled for children via `cgroup.subtree_control`, and in v2 processes live only in leaf cgroups.

**systemd** owns the tree: slices (`system.slice`, `user.slice`), services and scopes are cgroups. So the right way to limit a service is with unit properties such as `MemoryMax=`, `CPUQuota=`, `TasksMax=` and `IOWeight=` (in a drop-in), and `systemd-run -p MemoryMax=... cmd` for ad-hoc commands. `systemd-cgls` shows the tree and `systemd-cgtop` live usage per group.

Container runtimes create one cgroup per container: `docker run --memory 512m` simply writes `memory.max`. Inside a container, `/proc/self/cgroup` shows which group you are in, and applications should read limits from there rather than from total host memory.
concepts.code:
findmnt -t cgroup2                  # /sys/fs/cgroup  cgroup2  ...
cat /proc/self/cgroup               # 0::/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-3.scope
systemd-cgls --no-pager | head      # tree of slices, services and scopes
systemd-cgtop                       # live CPU/memory per cgroup
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/nginx.service/memory.current
# Limit a service (sudo systemctl edit myapp):
#   [Service]
#   MemoryMax=512M
#   CPUQuota=50%
#   TasksMax=200
systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=200M -p CPUQuota=25% ./batch-job.sh
# The raw interface that systemd and container runtimes use:
sudo mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/demo
echo 100M | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.max
echo "50000 100000" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.max    # half a CPU
echo $$ | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.procs          # move this shell in
takeaways: cgroup v2 is a directory tree at /sys/fs/cgroup; files are the API
memory.max, cpu.max, io.max and pids.max set limits
Use systemd properties (MemoryMax=, CPUQuota=) rather than writing files by hand
pitfalls: Sizing a JVM or worker pool from host memory inside a container instead of the cgroup's memory.max.

quiz.q: What does writing `50000 100000` to cpu.max do?
options: Allows 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period: half a CPU
quiz.explain: cpu.max is quota then period in microseconds.

quiz.q: A container hits its memory limit. What usually happens?
options: The kernel OOM-kills a process inside that cgroup
quiz.explain: Exceeding memory.max triggers the OOM killer within that cgroup.

concepts.name: System calls and tracing with strace
concepts.summary: See exactly what a program asks the kernel to do with strace, and when to reach for lsof, perf and eBPF tools.
concepts.why: When logs say nothing, tracing system calls reveals the missing file, the hanging connection or the permission problem.
concepts.body:
Programs cannot touch files, network or other processes directly: they ask the kernel through **system calls** such as `openat`, `read`, `write`, `connect`, `execve`, `clone` and `mmap`. Watching those calls shows what a program really does, regardless of language.

`strace` traces them:

- `strace cmd` prints every call with arguments and return value; errors appear as `= -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)`,
- `-f` follows child processes and threads, `-p PID` attaches to a running process,
- `-e trace=openat,connect` or classes like `%file`, `%network`, `%process` filter,
- `-T` shows time spent in each call, `-tt` timestamps, `-c` a summary table, `-o file` writes to a file, `-s 200` shows longer strings.

Classic uses: finding which config file a program looks for (`ENOENT` on `openat`), seeing why it gets `EACCES`, discovering which host or port a hung program waits on (`connect`, `poll`), and following which commands a script executes (`-e trace=execve -f`).

strace relies on **ptrace** and slows the traced program considerably, so be careful in production. Related tools: `ltrace` for library calls, `lsof -p PID` for open files and sockets, `/proc/PID/stack` and `wchan` for where a blocked task waits, `perf top` / `perf record` for CPU profiling. For low-overhead tracing in production, eBPF tools such as **bpftrace** and the BCC collection (`opensnoop`, `execsnoop`, `tcpconnect`) observe the same events system-wide.
concepts.code:
strace -c ls / > /dev/null          # summary: calls, errors and time per syscall
strace -e trace=openat,read cat /etc/hostname
# openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY) = 3
# read(3, "web1\n", 131072)              = 5
strace -f -e trace=execve bash -c 'ls | wc -l' 2>&1 | grep execve   # every program run
strace -e trace=%file -o trace.txt ./app; grep ENOENT trace.txt    # missing files
sudo strace -p 1234 -f -T -e trace=%network   # attach: what is it waiting on?
sudo lsof -p 1234 -a -i             # its network sockets
sudo cat /proc/1234/stack           # kernel stack of a blocked task
sudo perf top                       # where CPU time goes, kernel and user space
